In '111. No bad karma with regard to the body', what insight is conveyed by the reflection on: 'midst stillness near dawn,...'?

The text reflects: *"In the midst of the stillness near dawn, free of the noise of people or traffic—even the leaves of the trees were still, the air was cool, with a gentle drizzle falling like snow—Luang Pu, a member of the pure, noble Saṅgha, dropped his body, leaving us with only his virtues to remember and miss in a way that will know no end."* This passage points directly to the heart of experiential practice: letting go of superficial concepts and tuning awareness to the immediate truth of the moment. By investigating experience with honesty and forbearance (*khanti*), we discover an unshakable inner refuge that remains undisturbed by the worldly winds.

How does '111. No bad karma with regard to the body' characterize the nature of consciousness and the knowing mind?

The text observes: *"Always fully mindful and alert, he suffered no senility or forgetful lapses at all."* Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is not an independent 'soul' or enduring self; it arises in dependence on contact (*phassa*) and sense objects. The practice is to distinguish between the passing objects of awareness (thoughts, feelings, sensations) and the pure, unattached quality of 'the one who knows' (*poo roo*), resting in unconditioned peace.
